section.heading: Graph Inequalities on the Number Line
section.paragraph: Do you remember what it means for a number to be a solution to an equation? A solution of an equation is a value of a variable that makes a true statement when substituted into the equation.

What about the solution of an inequality? What number would make the inequality $$x > 3$$ true? Are you thinking, ‘x could be 4’? That’s correct, but x could be 5 too, or 20, or even 3.001. Any number greater than 3 is a solution to the inequality $$x > 3$$ .

We show the solutions to the inequality $$x > 3$$ on the number line by shading in all the numbers to the right of 3, to show that all numbers greater than 3 are solutions. Because the number 3 itself is not a solution, we put an open parenthesis at 3. The graph of $$x > 3$$ is shown in Figure 2.7. Please note that the following convention is used: thick arrows point in the positive direction and thin arrows point in the negative direction.

image.alt: This figure is a number line ranging from negative 5 to 5 with tick marks for each integer. The inequality x is greater than 3 is graphed on the number line, with an open parenthesis at x equals 3, and a red line extending to the right of the parenthesis.

figure.caption: The inequality $$x > 3$$ is graphed on this number line.

section.paragraph: The graph of the inequality $$x \geq 3$$ is very much like the graph of $$x > 3$$ , but now we need to show that 3 is a solution, too. We do that by putting a bracket at $$x = 3$$ , as shown in Figure 2.8.

image.alt: This figure is a number line ranging from negative 5 to 5 with tick marks for each integer. The inequality x is greater than or equal to 3 is graphed on the number line, with an open bracket at x equals 3, and a red line extending to the right of the bracket.

figure.caption: The inequality $$x \geq 3$$ is graphed on this number line.

section.paragraph: Notice that the open parentheses symbol, (, shows that the endpoint of the inequality is not included. The open bracket symbol, [, shows that the endpoint is included.

list.item: ⓐ $$x \leq 1$$ This means all numbers less than or equal to 1. We shade in all the numbers on the number line to the left of 1 and put a bracket at $$x = 1$$ to show that it is included.
ⓑ $$x < 5$$ This means all numbers less than 5, but not including 5. We shade in all the numbers on the number line to the left of 5 and put a parenthesis at $$x = 5$$ to show it is not included.

ⓒ $$x > - 1$$ This means all numbers greater than $$-1$$ , but not including $$-1$$ . We shade in all the numbers on the number line to the right of $$-1$$ , then put a parenthesis at $$x = -1$$ to show it is not included.

section.paragraph: We can also represent inequalities using interval notation. As we saw above, the inequality $$x > 3$$ means all numbers greater than 3. There is no upper end to the solution to this inequality. In interval notation, we express $$x > 3$$ as $$\left( {3,\infty} \right).$$ The symbol $$\infty$$ is read as ‘infinity’. It is not an actual number. Figure 2.9 shows both the number line and the interval notation.

image.alt: This figure is a number line ranging from negative 5 to 5 with tick marks for each integer. The inequality x is greater than 3 is graphed on the number line, with an open parenthesis at x equals 3, and a red line extending to the right of the parenthesis. The inequality is also written in interval notation as parenthesis, 3 comma infinity, parenthesis.

figure.caption: The inequality $$x > 3$$ is graphed on this number line and written in interval notation.

section.paragraph: The inequality $$x \leq 1$$ means all numbers less than or equal to 1. There is no lower end to those numbers. We write $$x \leq 1$$ in interval notation as $$\left( {-\infty,\left. 1 \right\rbrack} \right.$$ . The symbol $$-\infty$$ is read as ‘negative infinity’. Figure 2.10 shows both the number line and interval notation.

image.alt: This figure is a number line ranging from negative 5 to 5 with tick marks for each integer. The inequality x is less than or equal to 1 is graphed on the number line, with an open bracket at x equals 1, and a red line extending to the left of the bracket. The inequality is also written in interval notation as parenthesis, negative infinity comma 1, bracket.

figure.caption: The inequality $$x \leq 1$$ is graphed on this number line and written in interval notation.

section.heading: Solve Inequalities using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Inequality
section.paragraph: The Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality state that if two quantities are equal, when we add or subtract the same amount from both quantities, the results will be equal.

note.title: Properties of Equality
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{lccl} \textbf{Subtraction Property of Equality} & & & \textbf{Addition Property of Equality} \\ { \text{For any numbers} a,b, \text{and} c,} & & & { \text{For any numbers} a,b, \text{and} c,} \\ \begin{array}{lrll} \text{if} & a & = & {b,} \\ \text{then} & {a - c} & = & {b - c.} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{lrll} \text{if} & a & = & {b,} \\ \text{then} & {a + c} & = & {b + c.} \end{array} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Similar properties hold true for inequalities.

row.cell: For example, we know that −4 is less than 2.
If we subtract 5 from both quantities, is theleft side still less than the right side?
We get −9 on the left and −3 on the right.
And we know −9 is less than −3.
The inequality sign stayed the same.

section.paragraph: Similarly we could show that the inequality also stays the same for addition.
This leads us to the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Inequality.

note.title: Properties of Inequality
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{lccl} \textbf{Subtraction Property of Inequality} & & & \textbf{Addition Property of Inequality} \\ { \text{For any numbers} a,b, \text{and} c,} & & & { \text{For any numbers} a,b, \text{and} c,} \\ \begin{array}{cclrll} & & \text{if} & a & < & b \\ & & \text{then} & {a - c} & < & {b - c.} \\ & & & & & \\ & & \text{if} & a & > & b \\ & & \text{then} & {a - c} & > & {b - c.} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{cclrll} & & \text{if} & a & < & b \\ & & \text{then} & {a + c} & < & {b + c.} \\ & & & & & \\ & & \text{if} & a & > & b \\ & & \text{then} & {a + c} & > & {b + c.} \end{array} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: We use these properties to solve inequalities, taking the same steps we used to solve equations. Solving the inequality $$x + 5 > 9$$ , the steps would look like this:

row.cell: Subtract 5 from both sides to isolate $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Any number greater than 4 is a solution to this inequality.

section.heading: Solve Inequalities using the Division and Multiplication Properties of Inequality
section.paragraph: The Division and Multiplication Properties of Equality state that if two quantities are equal, when we divide or multiply both quantities by the same amount, the results will also be equal (provided we don’t divide by 0).

note.title: Properties of Equality
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{lccl} \textbf{Division Property of Equality} & & & \textbf{Multiplication Property of Equality} \\ { \text{For any numbers} a,b,c, \text{and} c \neq 0,} & & & { \text{For any real numbers} a,b,c,} \\ { \begin{array}{llll} \text{if} & a & = & {b,} \\ \text{then} & \frac{a}{c} & = & {\frac{b}{c}.} \end{array}} & & & { \begin{array}{llll} \text{if} & a & = & {b,} \\ \text{then} & {ac} & = & {bc.} \end{array}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Are there similar properties for inequalities? What happens to an inequality when we divide or multiply both sides by a constant?
Consider some numerical examples.
$$\textbf{The inequality signs stayed the same.}$$
Does the inequality stay the same when we divide or multiply by a negative number?
$$\textbf{The inequality signs reversed their direction.}$$
When we divide or multiply an inequality by a positive number, the inequality sign stays the same. When we divide or multiply an inequality by a negative number, the inequality sign reverses.
Here are the Division and Multiplication Properties of Inequality for easy reference.

note.source_type: Division and Multiplication Properties of Inequality
note.title: Division and Multiplication Properties of Inequality
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ { \text{For any real numbers} a,b,c} \\ \\ \\ \\ \begin{array}{l} { \text{if} a < b \text{and} c > 0, \text{then} \frac{a}{c} < \frac{b}{c} \text{and} ac < bc.} \\ { \text{if} a > b \text{and} c > 0, \text{then} \frac{a}{c} > \frac{b}{c} \text{and} ac > bc.} \\ { \text{if} a < b \text{and} c < 0, \text{then} \frac{a}{c} > \frac{b}{c} \text{and} ac > bc.} \\ { \text{if} a > b \text{and} c < 0, \text{then} \frac{a}{c} < \frac{b}{c} \text{and} ac < bc.} \end{array} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: When we divide or multiply an inequality by a:

list.item: positive number, the inequality stays the same.

note.title: Solving Inequalities
note.paragraph: Sometimes when solving an inequality, the variable ends up on the right. We can rewrite the inequality in reverse to get the variable to the left.
$$\begin{array}{ccl} & & {x > a \text{has the same meaning as} a < x} \end{array}$$
Think about it as “If Xavier is taller than Alex, then Alex is shorter than Xavier.”

section.heading: Solve Inequalities That Require Simplification
section.paragraph: Most inequalities will take more than one step to solve. We follow the same steps we used in the general strategy for solving linear equations, but be sure to pay close attention during multiplication or division.

problem.paragraph: Solve the inequality $$4m \leq 9m + 17$$ , graph the solution on the number line, and write the solution in interval notation.

row.cell: Subtract $$9m$$ from both sides to collect the variables on the left.
Divide both sides of the inequality by −5, and reverse the inequality.
Graph the solution on the number line.
Write the solution in interval notation.

section.paragraph: Just like some equations are identities and some are contradictions, inequalities may be identities or contradictions, too. We recognize these forms when we are left with only constants as we solve the inequality. If the result is a true statement, we have an identity. If the result is a false statement, we have a contradiction.

problem.paragraph: Solve the inequality $$8x - 2\left( {5 - x} \right) < 4\left( {x + 9} \right) + 6x$$ , graph the solution on the number line, and write the solution in interval notation.

row.cell: Simplify each side as much as possible.
Subtract $$10x$$ from both sides to collect the variables on the left.
The $$x$$ ’s are gone, and we have a true statement.
The inequality is an identity.The solution is all real numbers.
Graph the solution on the number line.
Write the solution in interval notation.

section.heading: Translate to an Inequality and Solve
section.paragraph: To translate English sentences into inequalities, we need to recognize the phrases that indicate the inequality. Some words are easy, like ‘more than’ and ‘less than’. But others are not as obvious.
Think about the phrase ‘at least’ – what does it mean to be ‘at least 21 years old’? It means 21 or more. The phrase ‘at least’ is the same as ‘greater than or equal to’.
Table 2.7 shows some common phrases that indicate inequalities.

row.cell: is greater than or equal to
is less than or equal to
